title: An old filter doesn't clean your water.
Activated carbon
body: The core of a pitcher filter cartridge is activated carbon, often made from coconut shells.
It is full of tiny pores. One gram has an internal surface area of over 500 m², bigger than a basketball court.

title: Odour, taste, chlorine
body: Chlorine, odours and some organic compounds stick to those pores. This is called adsorption.
The ion-exchange resin in the cartridge reduces some hardness, so limescale builds up in your kettle more slowly.

title: Bacteria and viruses
body: A standard carbon filter does not kill microbes.
It also barely removes dissolved substances like fluoride and nitrate.
So if your tap water is unsafe, a pitcher filter won't make it safe.

title: Chlorine gone, microbes stay
body: The filter removes chlorine, so nothing is left to keep bacteria in check.
Inside the wet carbon they settle in and multiply.
In a 2004 University of Arizona study, the highest bacteria counts were found in filtered water.

title: 3 simple rules
steps: Replace the cartridge at least every 4 weeks
Keep filtered water in the fridge
Drink it within a day, wash the pitcher often

title: Send this to one friend who doesn't know it.
accent: Especially if they own a filter pitcher.
